title: Judicial Renaissance -- Ch. 16: Abakada Guro Partylist v. Ermita: The Constitutionality of the E-Vat Law
keywords: 70 percent cap on creditable input tax
primary_topics: Chapter 16 of 'Judicial Renaissance' -- CJP's account of Abakada Guro Partylist v. Ermita, in which the Supreme Court by majority vote dismissed all five Petitions and upheld RA 9337, the Expanded Value-Added Tax Law, as constitutional in its entirety.

The procedural challenges and their rejection: the Court's refusal to go behind the enrolled bill to probe the Bicameral Conference Committee's work, and the Tolentino-based holdings on the no-amendment rule and the exclusive-origination rule for revenue bills.

The substantive challenges: whether the standby authority allowing the President, on the finance secretary's recommendation, to raise the VAT rate to 12 percent was an undue delegation, and whether the 70 percent input-tax cap, the 60-month amortization and the 5 percent withholding VAT violated due process, equal protection, uniformity and progressivity.

The spread of separate opinions -- Davide, Puno, Panganiban, Ynares-Santiago, Sandoval-Gutierrez, Callejo, Azcuna, Tinga and Chico-Nazario -- disputing the reach of the BCC's powers, the germaneness test and the constitutionality of particular sections.

CJP's own Separate Opinion: a partial grant voiding Sections 1, 2 and 3 as not germane to the House bills, acceptance of the standby authority as a mere fact-finding delegation, and insistence that the finance secretary remains the President's alter ego rather than an agent of Congress.
sub_topics: CJP opens by stating the holding -- RA 9337 is constitutional in its entirety in a Decision penned by Justice Ma. Alicia Austria-Martinez -- with a minority voting to strike specific provisions.

He notes the Court's unanimous Resolution holding former Finance Secretary Cesar V. Purisima guilty of indirect contempt and fining him P20,000 for media statements that placed the Court into dishonor, disrepute and discredit.

The facts: three bills restructuring the VAT, the Bicameral Conference Committee created to reconcile them, the enrolled bill signed into law on May 24, 2005, and the TRO issued on July 1, 2005, the law's effectivity date.

The Abakada and Pimentel petitions against Sections 4, 5 and 6, which authorized the President on the finance secretary's recommendation to raise the rate from 10 to 12 percent once VAT collections exceeded 2 4/5 percent of GDP or the deficit exceeded 1 1/2 percent.
The Pilipinas Shell Dealers petition against Sections 8 and 12 as arbitrary, oppressive, excessive and confiscatory, with the 70 percent input-tax cap attacked as regressive.
The Escudero group's attack on the BCC's deletion of the no-pass-on provisions and its insertion of 13 Sections found only in the Senate bill, contrary to exclusive origination.
Governor Enrique T. Garcia's contention that limiting the creditable input tax let VAT-registered entities retain collected taxes in violation of the public-purpose principle.

The Solicitor General's defense: presumption of constitutionality, the settled procedural rulings in Tolentino, the completeness of the law, and the E-VAT Law as the anchor of the government's fiscal reform agenda.
The Court's procedural rulings: even its expanded jurisdiction does not permit probing BCC irregularities behind an enrolled bill, since that concerns Congress's internal rules.
Its description of what a conference committee may do -- adopt one chamber's provisions, drop both, or compromise between disagreeing provisions.

Its reiteration that the no-amendment rule governs only each house's own procedure before transmittal, and that what must originate exclusively in the House is the revenue bill, not the law, leaving the Senate free to propose its own version.

On undue delegation, the Court's two-part test -- completeness and a sufficiently determinate standard -- and its holding, citing People v. Vera and Edu v. Ericta, that only the ascertainment of facts was delegated, the word 'shall' leaving the President no discretion.
The holding that the finance secretary in making the recommendation acts as agent of the legislative department, so that the President may not alter, modify or set aside the findings.

The rejection of the due process and equal protection attacks: the input tax may not exceed 70 percent of output tax, excess input tax remains creditable in later quarters or refundable through a tax credit certificate, and entitlement to the credit is a statutory privilege in which no one holds a vested right.
The Court's reasoning that the 60-month amortization only delays crediting while raising P22.6 billion a year, and that the 5 percent withholding VAT merely prescribes a method of collection.

The uniformity holding -- a standard rate applied without distinction among industries -- and the equitability holding based on the P1.5 million threshold and the continuing exemption of basic marine and agricultural food products.

The progressivity holding that the principle has no relation to VAT, which is paid equally regardless of income, and that the Constitution requires Congress only to evolve a progressive system of taxation.

Chief Justice Davide's opinion that the Senate's non-VAT amendments and the BCC's percentage and excise tax insertions were germane only to SB 1950 and had no leg to stand on, voting to strike Sections 1, 2, 3 and 14 to 18.

Justice Puno's five points: lack of ripeness, the limited powers of the BCC, which cannot act as a third house of Congress; grave abuse in deleting the pro-poor no-pass-on provision and inserting new restrictions on local government use of incremental revenue; and the overbreadth of the germaneness test.

CJP's Separate Opinion voting to partially grant the Petitions and declare Sections 1, 2 and 3 unconstitutional for amending corporate income tax rates, the tax credit on intercorporate dividends and the deduction for interest expense.

His qualification of the enrolled bill doctrine as non-absolute and yielding to mandatory constitutional provisions, and his view of the BCC as a mere creation of Congress bound by the origination, three-reading and no-amendment rules.
His acceptance of the standby authority as complete with fixed standards, making the President's role a mere ascertainment of facts and thus administrative rather than legislative.

His disagreement with the majority's characterization of the finance secretary as a projection of Congress, insisting the secretary remains the Chief Executive's alter ego and that Congress did not curtail the President's control over the Executive Department.

His conclusion that the BCC could validly delete the conflicting no-pass-on provisions but blatantly violated origination and germaneness in inserting income tax changes, and that the law's economic merits lie beyond judicial review.
Justice Ynares-Santiago's view that the BCC cannot compromise by introducing provisions absent from both bills, since an ad hoc committee cannot substitute for the will of Congress.

Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez's call to re-examine Tolentino's germaneness test, her view that Sections 4 to 6 were patently an invalid delegation with ineffectual and malleable standards, and her objection to the standby authority as a reward for satisfactory collection.
Justice Callejo's vote against the deletion of the no-pass-on provision and his charge that the ponencia effectively dismantled the three-reading and no-amendment rules.

Justice Azcuna's observation that one of the two conditions was certain to occur on January 1, 2006, his defense of germane mitigating measures, and his agreement that the corporate income tax provisions were not germane.

Justice Tinga's mixed vote: mandatory rather than discretionary presidential action, a qualified view of the finance secretary's agency, Section 21 as failing germaneness, the no-pass-on deletion as a valid compromise, and the 70 percent cap, the 60-month amortization and the 5 percent withholding VAT as unconstitutional threats to small and medium enterprises.

Justice Chico-Nazario's full concurrence, her warning that abandoning the enrolled bill doctrine would open a Pandora's Box, and her closing observation that the opposition to RA 9337 concerned its wisdom rather than its constitutionality.

stances.claim: There was no undue delegation of legislative power in the standby authority, because the law was complete and its standards fixed: once the factual or mathematical conditions occurred the President had no choice but to implement the 12 percent rate, making the role a mere ascertainment of facts.
stances.rhetorical_move: application of the two-part completeness-and-standard test, reinforced by the mandatory force of the word 'shall'

stances.claim: The finance secretary does not become an agent or projection of Congress in recommending the rate increase; the secretary remains the Chief Executive's alter ego, since RA 9337 did not restrict the President's constitutional control over the Executive Department.
stances.rhetorical_move: explicit disagreement with the majority, resolved by reading the mandate as merely asking the President, through the alter ego, to determine factual bases

stances.claim: The Bicameral Conference Committee, being a mere creation of Congress, may resolve differences only in conflicting provisions referred to it and only without violating the origination, three-reading and no-amendment rules; it blatantly violated origination and germaneness when it inserted the corporate income tax changes absent from the House versions.
stances.rhetorical_move: drawing a line between valid reconciliation (including deletion of conflicting no-pass-on provisions) and invalid insertion of non-germane subject matter

stances.claim: The enrolled bill doctrine is not absolute; it governs the internal rules and processes of lawmaking but must yield to mandatory provisions of the 1987 Constitution, leaving the Court the power and duty to strike down enactments made in violation of constitutional conditions.
stances.rhetorical_move: qualifying a settled doctrine rather than rejecting it, to preserve a narrow avenue of review

stances.claim: The advantages, disadvantages and long-term economic effects of the E-VAT Law are beyond the reach of judicial review.
stances.rhetorical_move: closing disclaimer separating constitutionality from wisdom, echoed by Justice Nazario's final observation

stances.claim: The 70 percent cap on creditable input tax, the 60-month amortization and the 5 percent withholding VAT would exterminate small and medium enterprises and are confiscatory, requiring the Court to cut the hangman's noose before the law takes effect.
stances.rhetorical_move: report of Justice Tinga's dissenting economic analysis, including the time-value-of-money argument

notable_anecdotes: The Court issued its TRO on July 1, 2005 -- the very day RA 9337 was to take effect -- effective immediately and until further orders.

Alongside the Decision the Court unanimously held former Finance Secretary Cesar V. Purisima in indirect contempt and fined him P20,000 for media statements that placed the Court and its members into dishonor, disrepute and discredit.
Justice Azcuna, working from figures supplied during the Oral Arguments, observed that one of the two conditions triggering the VAT increase was certain to be met on January 1, 2006.

Justice Tinga invoked the image of the Court stepping forth to cut the hangman's noose before the law's implementation, while Justice Nazario warned that abandoning the enrolled bill doctrine would open a Pandora's Box.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 16 of 'Judicial Renaissance' reports Abakada Guro Partylist v. Ermita, in which the Supreme Court, through a Decision penned by Justice Ma. Alicia Austria-Martinez, dismissed all five Petitions and upheld RA 9337, the Expanded Value-Added Tax Law, as constitutional in its entirety, while unanimously holding former Finance Secretary Cesar V. Purisima in indirect contempt and fining him P20,000 for statements that placed the Court into dishonor, disrepute and discredit. Justice Panganiban narrated the passage of the three bills, the Bicameral Conference Committee that reconciled them, the signing of the enrolled bill on May 24, 2005 and the TRO issued on July 1, the law's effectivity date. The petitioners attacked the standby authority in Sections 4, 5 and 6 allowing the President, on the finance secretary's recommendation, to raise the rate to 12 percent once VAT collections or the deficit crossed the specified fractions of GDP; the 70 percent cap on creditable input tax, the 60-month amortization and the 5 percent withholding VAT; and the BCC's deletion of the no-pass-on provisions and insertion of Senate-only sections contrary to exclusive origination. The Court refused to go behind the enrolled bill, reiterated Tolentino on the no-amendment and origination rules, applied the completeness-and-standard test to find only a delegation of fact-ascertainment, held that entitlement to input tax credit is a statutory privilege carrying no vested right, and ruled the law uniform, equitable and unaffected by the progressivity principle, which it said has no relation to VAT. Chief Justice Davide, and Justices Puno, Ynares-Santiago, Sandoval-Gutierrez, Callejo, Azcuna and Tinga wrote separately, variously arguing that the BCC cannot act as a third house of Congress, that the germaneness test is overbroad, that the no-pass-on deletion was invalid, and that the input-tax cap would exterminate small and medium enterprises. In his own Separate Opinion, Panganiban voted to void Sections 1, 2 and 3 as not germane to the House bills, treated the enrolled bill doctrine as non-absolute, accepted the standby authority as a complete delegation making the President's role administrative rather than legislative, disagreed with the majority's view of the finance secretary as an agent of Congress by insisting the secretary remains the President's alter ego, and concluded that the law's economic advantages and long-term effects lie beyond the reach of judicial review.
